Mitch McConnell was hospitalized on June 14. Over the next three months, the Kentucky senator was barely seen or heard, aside from two awkward “proof of life” photos and a statement explaining he’d suffered a fall that left him “briefly unconscious” and he then developed “a mild case of pneumonia.”
On Monday evening, the 84-year-old Republican finally returned to the Senate to cast the deciding vote on a federal appeals-court nominee. Though McConnell was surrounded by journalists and colleagues the whole time, somehow he was still barely seen or heard.
In a statement posted to his social-media feeds, McConnell said he was excited to “get back to more of business as usual” on behalf of his constituents.
“My recovery has been a long and often frustrating process, and the lingering effects of childhood polio haven’t made it any easier,” he wrote. “I’m still not quite back to 100%, but I’ve assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me.”
McConnell was considerably less verbose as aides moved him from his D.C. home to a van to head to the Capitol. In response to questions shouted by a gaggle of journalists and photographers, the senator waved and gave a thumbs-up:
He also smiled … a lot:
McConnell made brief remarks to the press outside the Senate chamber. Journalists were allowed to photograph the senator but were barred from recording video. As explained in a joint statement from the two groups that manage professional conduct for journalists covering Congress, reporters asked to film McConnell’s statement but their request was denied by the Senate Rules Committee … which the Kentuckian just happens to chair.
The former Republican Majority Leader didn’t take any questions, and his words were “hard to make out” at times, according to The Wall Street Journal:
“I must admit, after two years of — decades actually — of dodging your questions, I wasn’t sure how many of you would be here today,” McConnell, 84 years old, joked to reporters. His words weren’t clearly enunciated and at times were hard to make out. “Time to get back to work, to finish the job for this Congress,” he said, citing the farm bill and backing the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and Ukraine. He didn’t take any questions.
You can hear the senator’s remarks for yourself at the 35-second mark in the video below. But that’s only because a WHAS11 reporter recorded audio of McConnell’s statement:
In the same video, McConnell’s Republican colleague John Kennedy tells reporters that McConnell “looks great,” adding, “I told him that he has a new nickname. We’re going to call him Rock, as in ‘Like a rock.’”
That may be overstating things. But McConnell’s condition is definitely a lot better than Laura Loomer reported over the summer.
This piece was updated to note that the Senate Rules Committee did not allow journalists to film McConnell.

Kentucky Republican Senator Mitch McConnell's very spaced-out expression sparked a flurry of memes after he was filmed by TMZ being loaded into a car to go to the Senate after months of public questions surrounding his health.
The 84-year-old—who chairs the Senate Rules Committee—was found unconscious at his Washington residence in June, prompting an advanced life support response. Over the summer, his office said his condition was improving.
In a July 13 social media post, McConnell said he had been hospitalized after a fall that left him "briefly unconscious" and revealed he was also recovering from a mild case of pneumonia. He included a photo of himself in a hospital bed, but the image only intensified speculation online, with some users claiming it had been generated or manipulated using artificial intelligence.
McConnell's aides have declined to say whether they have recently spoken with him, adding to speculation about his condition. The Daily Beast reported that a semi-permanent security detail remained stationed at George Washington University Hospital, where McConnell received treatment.
Weeks later, the senator, who also spend time in a rehabilitation center, returned to cast a vote when the chamber decided on a nomination to fill a district court bench opening in Ohio. He assured voters that he will “do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me.”
But things did not look good when TMZ shared footage of McConnell being loaded into a car heading to Capitol Hill on Monday with his mouth agape.
You can see what happened in the video below.
Let's be real, this display really hasn't done anything to inspire our confidence in McConnell or GOP leadership—things look just as bad as expected, if not worse.
And like clockwork, social media users pounced to mock the entire situation and tell some harsh truths about McConnell's condition and his spaced-out expression.
It's way past time for the country to have a productive conversation and do something about term limits for our legislators.

After a 92-day absence, Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky) returned to Capitol Hill on Monday, despite lingering questions about his health and fitness to serve.
McConnell participated in votes on the Senate floor, including a vote on the advancement of a federal judge nominated by President Donald Trump. His renewed presence in the Senate is also imperative for Republicans on the Senate Agriculture Committee, as the conference has just a 12-11 advantage over Democrats on that panel.
Earlier in the day, TMZ captured video of McConnell exiting his D.C. home, showing the senator requiring assistance to enter his vehicle and buckle his seatbelt. McConnell appeared unresponsive to reporters’ questions.
Before taking part in Senate floor activities, McConnell addressed reporters inside the Capitol, though his staff forbade any recording of the senator during that time. Some media reports took note of his continued health issues — The Associated Press, for example, reported that McConnell was “looking noticeably more frail” than at his last public appearance, while CNN’s Manu Raju tweeted that the senator “appear[ed] frailer and his voice [was] slower.”
After speaking briefly to reporters, McConnell refused to take any questions. His office later released a statement, saying:
Today, I’ll cast my first Senate vote since I took a bad fall back in June. I look forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues.
“I’m still not quite back to 100 percent,” McConnell’s statement continued, “but I’ve assured [Senate Majority] Leader [John] Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me.”
The refusal to allow recording of the senator during his return to the Capitol means there has not been any audio recording of McConnell since earlier this summer.
On June 14, McConnell reportedly suffered a fall in his home, which required hospitalization and, soon after, a long period of physical rehabilitation. Despite releasing photographs and text statements, his failure to provide audio or video evidence of his health led to doubts about his ability to remain in office for the remainder of his term, which officially ends in January.
McConnell’s absence could reasonably be viewed as a long-term “sick leave,” as he was still receiving compensation despite being away from his work as a senator for the past three months. The U.S. is the only wealthy country in the world that doesn’t guarantee even a single day of paid sick leave for its workers. Notably, McConnell has been instrumental in voting against and blocking efforts to implement such protections, including during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic.

One of the mainstays of America’s legislative branch was seen roaming the corridors of the U.S. Capitol building, as the spirit of Mitch McConnell returned to the Senate [in what has been described as an act of Disney].
The Kentucky senator had been out of the public eye for several months but made his long-awaited return to work this week, as his ethereal presence appeared on the Senate floor to give an inspirational speech to his colleagues [or at least those with the psychic gifts to perceive his aura] ahead of the November midterm elections.
“Hello there,” McConnell’s spectral form said as it materialized in front of the podium. “I have returned to you for this important time. We have a lot of work ahead of us, and I’m proud to be back where I belong. Though I have become one with the Force, that won’t stop me from fulfilling my duties and my responsibility to represent the hardworking people of Kentucky. Mitch McConnell will be with you… always.”
McConnell’s colleagues said it was a relief to [sense his presence] to guide them during this dark time [and that when it was really dark it was even easier to see him. The former Senate leader, a staunch foe of President Trump’s SAVE America Act, is said to be laser-focused on the security of the upcoming midterm elections.
“All votes should be counted,” McConnell said, “including those of people falsely accused of being dead.]
